what_it_does: Pattern matching at high speed often relies on running many tiny rule machines — called finite state machines (FSMs) — simultaneously; each FSM reads an incoming stream of characters and reports whether its pattern has been seen. The problem is that at any given moment, for any given incoming character, the vast majority of these machines are simply waiting and doing nothing, yet existing hardware still wastes time and energy checking on all of them. Hopps is an accelerator that notices this idleness — it tracks only the machines that are actually active for each incoming symbol, skips the dormant ones entirely, and fetches the transition rules for active machines in efficient bursts from fast on-chip memory (a small, quick scratchpad). The result is that the hardware work done per incoming character scales with how many machines are actually active rather than the total count, which can be a large saving when most machines are idle.
